I wanted a simple setup where GitHub stays my main repo, but GitLab always has a full backup. Any push to GitHub should automatically appear in GitLab—branches, tags, deletions, everything.
GitLab offers pull mirroring, but it requires a paid subscription. This post demonstrates a free, production-safe solution using GitHub Actions.
GitLab offers pull mirroring, but it requires a paid subscription. This post demonstrates a free, production-safe solution using GitHub Actions.
What this setup does (and doesn’t) Does:
Automatically sync GitHub → GitLab Mirrors all branches and tags Deletes branches in GitLab if deleted in GitHub Works on GitLab Free Does not:
Sync GitLab back to GitHub Allow manual pushes to GitLab Step 1: Create an Empty GitLab Repository Go to GitLab and create a new project. Choose a blank project (do not initialize with README). Set visibility as desired (private is fine). Step 2: Create a GitLab Access Token Go to GitLab → Preferences → Access Tokens. Create a token with scope: write_repository. Copy the token (it will not be shown again). Step 3: Add Token to GitHub Secrets Go to GitHub repository → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions. Add a new secret named GITLAB_TOKEN. Paste the GitLab token as the value Step 4: Add GitHub Actions Workflow Create the file .github/workflows/main.yml in your GitHub repository and add the following code:
name: Mirror to GitLab on: push: jobs: gitlab-mirror: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: # "0" is crucial! It downloads the full history, not just the last commit. fetch-depth: 0 - name: Push to GitLab run: | # 1. Clean up any previous remote links git remote remove gitlab 2>/dev/null || true # 2. Add the GitLab remote # REPLACE WITH YOUR DETAILS BELOW git remote add gitlab https://oauth2:${{ secrets.GITLAB_TOKEN }}@gitlab.com/YOUR_GROUP/YOUR_PROJECT.git # We use --prune to delete branches on GitLab that I deleted on GitHub. # We explicitly push refs/heads (branches) and refs/tags (releases). git push --force --prune gitlab +refs/heads/*:refs/heads/* +refs/tags/*:refs/tags/* Step 5: Adjust GitLab Branch Protection Go to GitLab → Settings → Repository. Unprotect the main branch or allow force push for maintainers. Remove protected tags if any exist. Step 6: Test Commit and push the workflow file to GitHub. Open GitHub → Actions and confirm the workflow succeeds. Verify the repository is updated in GitLab. Best practices Use GitHub as source of truth. GitLab is read-only.Do not push code directly to GitLab. Use GitLab strictly as a backup mirror.

GitLab offers pull mirroring, but it requires a paid subscription. This post demonstrates a free, production-safe solution using GitHub Actions.

SOLID principles were introduced by Robert C.Martin (Uncle Bob). - Robert Cecil Martin
What does SOLID stand for?
S – Single Responsibility Principle
A class should have one and only one reason to change, meaning that a class should have only one job
O – Open Closed Principle
Software entities (classes, modules, functions, etc.) should be open for extension but closed for modification.
L – Liskov Substitution Principle
Every subclass or derived class should be substitutable for its base or parent class
I – Interface Segregation Principle
Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.
D – Dependency Inversion Principle
Entities must depend on abstractions, not on concretions.
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules, both should depend on abstractions.
Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Linq; using System.Text; using System.Threading.Tasks; namespace FactorialNumber\_ForLoop { class Program { static void Main(string\[\] args) { int number, fact = 1; Console.WriteLine("Enter the number"); number = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine()); for (int i = number; i >=1; i--) { fact = fact \* i; } Console.WriteLine("{0} Factorial is {1}",number,fact); } } } Output: Enter the number 5 5 Factorial is 120

Find factorial of a number in C#

    using System;
    using System.Collections.Generic;
    using System.Linq;
    using System.Text;
    using System.Threading.Tasks;

    namespace FactorialNumber\_ForLoop
    {
        class Program
        {
            static void Main(string\[\] args)
            {
                int number, fact = 1;
                Console.WriteLine("Enter the number");
                number = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());

                for (int i = number; i >=1; i--)
                {
                    fact = fact \* i;
                }
                Console.WriteLine("{0} Factorial is {1}",number,fact);
            }
        }
    }

Output: Enter the number 5 5 Factorial is 120

Find factorial of a number in C# using recursion
using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Linq; using System.Text; using System.Threading.Tasks; namespace FactorialNumber\_Recursion { class Program { static void Main(string\[\] args) { int number =0; Console.WriteLine("Enter the number"); number = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine()); int fact = Factorial(number); Console.WriteLine("{0} Factorial is {1}", number, fact); } public static int Factorial(int num) { if (num ==0) { return 1; } else { return (num \* Factorial(num - 1)); } } } } Output: Enter the number 5 5 Factorial is 120
summary:
Find factorial of a number in C# using recursion

    using System;
    using System.Collections.Generic;
    using System.Linq;
    using System.Text;
    using System.Threading.Tasks;

    namespace FactorialNumber\_Recursion
    {
        class Program
        {
            static void Main(string\[\] args)
            {
                int number =0;

                Console.WriteLine("Enter the number");
                number = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());
                int fact = Factorial(number);
                Console.WriteLine("{0} Factorial is {1}", number, fact);
            }

            public static int Factorial(int num)
            {
                if (num ==0)
                {
                    return 1;
                }
                else
                {
                    return (num \* Factorial(num - 1));
                }
            }
        }
    }

Output: Enter the number 5 5 Factorial is 120
title: C# Program - How to find factorial of a number in  C# using recursion  ?

Mediates between the domain and data mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects. by Edward Hieatt and Rob Mee
The Repository Pattern is a common construct to avoid duplication of data access logic throughout our application. The Repository pattern adds a separation layer between the data and domain layers of an application.
Why Use Repository Pattern : Increase test-ability and have a loose coupling to underlying persistence technology. Improve the code’s maintainability and readability by separating business logic from data or service access logic. References
http://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/repository.html http://www.remondo.net/repository-pattern-example-csharp/ http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ff649690.aspx
